questions.stem: Which hypothesis could be tested in a school laboratory investigation?
options: If the acid is warmer, magnesium will react with it faster
Magnesium is the most interesting metal to react with hydrochloric acid
Hydrochloric acid should always be handled very carefully in schools
Chemical reactions happen because particles want to be more stable
questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis predicts a relationship between an independent variable (temperature) and a measurable dependent variable (rate). Opinions, safety advice and statements about what particles want cannot be tested by experiment.

questions.stem: A student writes the hypothesis 'Catalysts make reactions better.' Why should it be rewritten?
options: It names too many independent variables, so the results would be confusing
It is written as a statement, but a hypothesis must be written as a question
It refers to catalysts, which cannot be used in a school laboratory
It does not name a measurable dependent variable, so it cannot be tested
questions.explanation: 'Better' could mean faster, cheaper or a higher yield, so there is nothing definite to measure. A testable version would be, for example, 'Adding manganese dioxide will increase the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.'

questions.stem: A student's hypothesis is that all metal oxides catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Tests show that one oxide speeds up the reaction but another has no effect. What should the student do?
options: Modify the hypothesis to fit the evidence, then test the new version
Keep the hypothesis, because one of the results supports it
Leave out the result that disagrees and repeat with the first oxide
Accept the hypothesis as a theory, because it has now been tested
questions.explanation: Evidence that contradicts a hypothesis means it must be revised, for example to name the oxides that act as catalysts, and then tested again. Ignoring inconvenient results is poor and unethical practice.

questions.stem: A student measures the volume of CO₂ released in 2 minutes when marble of different particle sizes reacts with acid. What is the dependent variable?
options: The 2 minute time allowed for each trial
The volume of CO₂ released in 2 minutes
The particle size of the marble used
The concentration of the acid used
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to changes in the independent variable. Here the particle size is deliberately changed (independent), and the gas volume is measured (dependent).

questions.stem: In the investigation of marble particle size and the volume of CO₂ released, which set of variables should be controlled?
options: Particle size of marble, volume of acid, and volume of gas produced
Volume of gas produced, time allowed, and particle size of marble
Colour of the marble, shape of the flask, and time of day
Mass of marble, volume and concentration of acid, and temperature
questions.explanation: Every variable that could affect the volume of gas, apart from particle size, must be kept the same so that the test is valid. Particle size is the independent variable and gas volume is the dependent variable, so neither is controlled.

questions.stem: A student tests whether adding copper(II) sulfate speeds up the reaction of zinc with acid. Why is a flask containing only zinc and acid also set up?
options: It gives a baseline, so any change can be linked to the CuSO₄
It doubles the number of trials, which makes the results more accurate
It checks that the zinc and acid are not contaminated with copper ions
It lets the student measure the copper produced in the other flask
questions.explanation: An experimental control is identical except that the factor being tested is left out. Comparing with it shows whether the copper(II) sulfate causes the change, rather than some other factor.

questions.stem: An investigation is described as valid. What does this mean?
options: It tests what it set out to test, as a fair test
It gives similar results each time the same method is repeated
Its results are close to the true or accepted value
Its measurements are close to one another, with little spread
questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the method actually investigates the question, which requires fair testing with controlled variables. Repeatability describes reliability, closeness to the true value is accuracy, and small spread is precision.

questions.stem: How is reliable primary data obtained?
options: By changing several variables at once to collect more data
By repeating trials and checking that the results are consistent
By using the most expensive equipment available in the laboratory
By doing one careful trial and recording many decimal places
questions.explanation: Data are reliable when repeated measurements agree. Repeating trials shows the spread of results and allows outliers to be identified. A single trial gives no evidence of consistency, however carefully it is done.

questions.stem: A student needs a reliable value for the density of aluminium. Which secondary source is most reliable?
options: A school assignment written by a student in an earlier year
A data book of physical constants published by a scientific society
A social media video in which an influencer measures the density
An anonymous website with no references for any of its figures
questions.explanation: Reliable secondary sources are authoritative, checked by experts and cite where their data come from. A recognised data book meets these tests; anonymous or unchecked sources may contain errors.

questions.stem: In a risk assessment, what distinguishes a hazard from a risk?
options: A hazard can cause harm; risk is how likely and severe harm is
A hazard is a minor danger; a risk is a major danger to everyone
A hazard applies to chemicals; a risk applies only to equipment
A hazard is the harm done; risk is the first-aid response to it
questions.explanation: Concentrated acid is a hazard. The risk depends on how likely it is to cause harm and how serious that harm would be, and control measures are chosen to reduce the risk.

questions.stem: Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off corrosive fumes. Which control measure is most appropriate?
options: Use it near an open window, so the fumes blow away quickly
Heat it gently first, so the fumes are given off before use
Dilute it by adding water to the acid in a sealed container
Use it in a fume cupboard, wearing safety glasses and gloves
questions.explanation: A fume cupboard removes the fumes from the working area, and eye and skin protection guard against splashes. Heating acid would release more fumes, and diluting in a sealed container is unsafe.

questions.stem: A student needs to measure exactly 25.00 mL of a solution for a titration. Which piece of equipment should be used?
options: A 250 mL conical flask
A 25.00 mL volumetric pipette
A 50 mL measuring cylinder
A 100 mL beaker with graduations
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume with a small uncertainty, such as ±0.03 mL. Measuring cylinders and beaker graduations are far less precise.

questions.stem: A company pays for a study into the safety of its own pesticide. Which ethical issue does this raise?
options: A breach of copyright, because the company owns the pesticide
A problem of reliability, because only one pesticide is studied
A conflict of interest that could bias the reported results
A risk that the pesticide will react with the laboratory equipment
questions.explanation: When the funder benefits from a particular result, there is a risk that unfavourable findings are played down. Disclosing funding and independent peer review help to manage this conflict of interest.

questions.stem: Concentrated acid splashes onto a student's hand. What should be done first?
options: Rinse the area under plenty of running water
Neutralise it with sodium hydroxide solution
Wipe it off with a dry paper towel and continue
Cover it with a bandage to keep the area clean
questions.explanation: Flushing with large amounts of water dilutes and removes the acid quickly. Adding a base could cause a further reaction that releases heat and damages the skin.

questions.stem: How should the volume of a solution in a burette be read?
options: At eye level, from the top edge of the meniscus
At eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus
From above, at the top edge of the meniscus
From below, at the middle of the meniscus
questions.explanation: For aqueous solutions the meniscus curves downwards, and its bottom is read with the eye level with it to avoid parallax error. Reading from above or below gives a value that is too high or too low.

questions.stem: A reaction releases 4.5 × 10⁶ J of energy. How is this written using a scale prefix?
options: 4.5 GJ
4.5 kJ
4.5 MJ
questions.explanation: Mega (M) means 10⁶, so 4.5 × 10⁶ J is 4.5 MJ. Giga (G) is 10⁹ and kilo (k) is 10³.

questions.stem: The radius of a chlorine atom is about 100 pm. What is this in metres?
questions.explanation: Pico (p) means 10⁻¹², so 100 pm = 100 × 10⁻¹² m = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. 1 × 10⁻¹² m is just one picometre.

questions.stem: Which scale prefix stands for 10¹⁵?
options: Peta (P)
Tera (T)
Giga (G)
Femto (f)
questions.explanation: Peta is 10¹⁵, tera 10¹² and giga 10⁹. Femto is the small prefix 10⁻¹⁵, so it has the same power but the opposite sign.

questions.stem: A student compares the energy released when five different fuels are burnt. Which way of presenting the results is most appropriate?
options: A column graph, because the independent variable is categorical
A line graph, because the independent variable is continuous
A pie chart, because the results add up to a total of 100%
A scatter graph with a single line of best fit through all fuels
questions.explanation: The fuels are separate categories with no values in between, so a column graph is used. A line graph or line of best fit suits continuous independent variables such as temperature or concentration.

questions.stem: Why should a student acknowledge secondary sources using a referencing style?
options: To make the report longer and more impressive to the reader
To prove that the student's own results were the same as the sources
To avoid needing to analyse the data from those sources
To credit the authors and let readers find and check the sources
questions.explanation: Referencing gives credit for others' work, avoids plagiarism and lets readers judge the reliability of the sources for themselves.

questions.stem: Three titres are 22.15 mL, 22.25 mL and 22.20 mL. What are the mean and the range?
options: Mean 22.20 mL, range 0.10 mL
Mean 22.20 mL, range 0.05 mL
Mean 22.25 mL, range 0.10 mL
Mean 22.15 mL, range 0.05 mL

questions.stem: Three measurements are 20.10, 20.20 and 20.30 mL. What is their sample standard deviation (dividing by n − 1)?
questions.explanation: The mean is 20.20 mL and the squared deviations are 0.01, 0 and 0.01, summing to 0.02. Dividing by n − 1 = 2 gives 0.01, and √0.01 = 0.10 mL. Dividing by n instead gives 0.082 mL, and 0.20 mL is the range.

questions.stem: Two groups measure the same titre. Group A's results have a standard deviation of 0.05 mL and group B's 0.40 mL. What does this show?
options: Group B's results are more valid, because their spread is larger
Group A's results are more precise, with less spread about the mean
Group A's results are more accurate, being closer to the true value
Group B's results are more precise, with a wider spread about the mean
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures the spread of results about the mean: the smaller it is, the more precise the data. It says nothing about accuracy, because both groups could share the same systematic error.

questions.stem: In a rate experiment, the times for a cross to disappear are 42 s, 44 s, 61 s and 43 s. Which value is an outlier?
options: 44 s, because it is the closest to the mean of all four
None, because every measured value must be averaged
61 s, because it lies well outside the others
42 s, because it is the lowest of the four values
questions.explanation: Three results agree within 2 s, but 61 s is far from them, perhaps from a timing or mixing error. Outliers should be checked, and left out of the mean only with a stated reason.

questions.stem: A 25.00 mL pipette has an uncertainty of ±0.03 mL. What is the percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty/measured value × 100 = 0.03/25.00 × 100 = 0.12%. Leaving out the × 100 gives 0.0012.

questions.stem: Each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 mL. A titre found from an initial and a final reading is 20.00 mL. What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?
questions.explanation: A titre is the difference of two readings, so their uncertainties add: ±0.10 mL. Percentage uncertainty = 0.10/20.00 × 100 = 0.50%. Using only one reading's uncertainty gives 0.25%.

questions.stem: Five measurements of the boiling point of pure water at 100 kPa are 96.1, 96.0, 96.2, 96.1 and 96.1 °C. The accepted value is 99.6 °C. How are the results best described?
options: Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: The values agree closely with each other (precise) but are all about 3.5 °C below the accepted value (not accurate). This pattern points to a systematic error, such as a faulty thermometer.

questions.stem: A balance reads 0.12 g with nothing on it, and the student does not zero it. What kind of error is this?
options: A systematic error, making every mass 0.12 g too low
A random error that repeated trials would cancel out
A systematic error, making every mass 0.12 g too high
A random error, making masses vary unpredictably
questions.explanation: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so it is systematic. Repeating trials does not remove it; zeroing (taring) the balance does.

questions.stem: In the disappearing cross experiment, a student sometimes stops the timer slightly early and sometimes slightly late. What kind of error is this?
options: Systematic error, which shifts all the times in the same direction
Random error, which can be reduced by repeating and averaging
Systematic error, which can be reduced by repeating and averaging
Random error, which can only be removed by changing the method
questions.explanation: Judging the moment by eye varies unpredictably in both directions, so it is random error. Averaging several trials reduces its effect; a light sensor would reduce it further.

questions.stem: A student calculates 2.0 × 3.456. How should the answer be written to the correct number of significant figures?
questions.explanation: When multiplying, the answer has as many significant figures as the least precise value. 2.0 has two significant figures, so 6.912 is rounded to 6.9.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.004060 g?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant. The digits 4, 0, 6 and the final 0 are significant, because a trailing zero after the decimal point shows the precision of the measurement.

questions.stem: When the concentration of sodium thiosulfate is doubled, the time for the cross to disappear halves. What is the relationship between concentration and time?
options: Inversely proportional
Directly proportional
No relationship
Exponential growth
questions.explanation: Doubling one variable halves the other, so concentration × time is constant: they are inversely proportional. The rate, which is proportional to 1/time, is directly proportional to concentration.

questions.stem: The solubility of a salt is measured at 20, 40 and 60 °C. Why is a prediction of its solubility at 90 °C less reliable than one at 30 °C?
options: It extrapolates beyond the measured range, assuming the trend continues
It interpolates between measured points, which always adds random error
Solubility cannot be measured at temperatures above about 60 °C
Higher temperatures always give lower solubility than predicted
questions.explanation: A value at 30 °C lies between measured points (interpolation), while 90 °C lies outside the data (extrapolation). The trend may change outside the measured range, so extrapolated predictions are less certain.

questions.stem: A rate investigation is done at room temperature, but the room warms during the day and the results are inconsistent. Which improvement is best?
options: Do all the trials faster so that the room has no time to warm up
Record the room temperature at the start of the day only
Use a larger flask so the reaction mixture stays cooler
Carry out every trial in a thermostatically controlled water bath
questions.explanation: Temperature affects rate, so it must be controlled. A water bath keeps every trial at the same temperature, improving validity and reliability.

questions.stem: The ideal gas model treats gas particles as having no volume and no attractions. Why is it still useful even though real gases differ?
options: It describes real gases exactly, so its predictions never need checking
It applies to solids and liquids as well, so it explains every state
It was proposed by a famous scientist, so it is accepted without testing
It predicts real gases well, except at high pressure or low temperature
questions.explanation: Models simplify reality. Real gas particles do have volume and weak attractions, which matter when particles are crowded or slow, but under ordinary conditions the ideal gas model's predictions are close to measured values.

questions.stem: Scientific knowledge is said to be both contestable and testable. What does this mean?
options: It can be checked by experiment and revised when new evidence emerges
It is decided by a vote among scientists and changes with each vote
It is fixed once published, but different scientists may interpret it
It applies only to the conditions of the original experiment
questions.explanation: Scientific ideas make predictions that can be tested, and they are revised or replaced when better evidence appears, as models of the atom were from Dalton to Rutherford and beyond.

questions.stem: What does peer review contribute to science?
options: Students in the same class mark each other's practical reports for grades
Independent experts check methods, data and conclusions before publication
The scientists who did the work review it again before sending it to print
Members of the public vote on whether the findings should be accepted
questions.explanation: In peer review, other experts in the field scrutinise a paper's methods, data analysis and conclusions, helping to catch errors and unsupported claims before the work is published.

questions.stem: Which value is written in correct scientific notation?
questions.explanation: Scientific notation has exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point, multiplied by a power of 10. The other forms have the same value but do not follow this convention.
